syllabus_version: Issue 4 (as on the cover; footer 'Specification – Issue 4 – September 2024'). Pearson Edexcel International GCSE in Physics (4PH1), first teaching September 2017, first examination June 2019. Page numbers in this map are the printed page numbers; PDF page = printed page + 6.
tier_notes: Untiered (p. 1). All students take both papers in the same series (pp. 1, 8). Paper 1 (4PH1/1P) 'Assesses core content that is not in bold and does not have a ‘P’ reference'; Paper 2 (4PH1/2P) 'Assesses all the content, including content that is in bold and has a ‘P’ reference ... Statements in bold cover some sub-topics in greater depth' (pp. 8-9, 29). Questions may come from any topic area across the specification. Total 180 marks (110 + 70), papers not scaled; grades 9 to 1, individual papers not graded (pp. 29, 35). Pipeline tier field: core = Paper 1 and Paper 2 content (no P suffix); supplement = Paper 2 only (P suffix, bold). Website labels: 'Paper 1 & 2' and 'Paper 2 only'.
paper_notes: Both papers: 'A combination of different question styles, including multiple-choice questions, short-answer questions, calculations and extended open-response questions.' A calculator may be used (pp. 8-9, 29).
Paper 1: 2-hour written examination, 110 marks, 61.1% of the qualification; content not in bold without a 'P' reference. Paper code also 4SD0/1P (shared with Science Double Award) (pp. 8, 39).
Paper 2: 1 hour 15 minutes, 70 marks, 38.9%; all content including bold 'P' statements (pp. 9, 29).
Availability: November and June; first assessment June 2019 (pp. 8-9).

Experimental skills are assessed through the written examinations: solve problems in a practical context; apply knowledge in questions with a practical context; devise and plan investigations; demonstrate or describe experimental methods including safe techniques; make observations and measurements with appropriate precision, record and present them; identify independent, dependent and control variables; analyse and interpret data to draw conclusions; communicate findings using technical language, calculations and graphs; assess reliability; evaluate data and methods (p. 30).

AO weightings (p. 31): AO1 Knowledge and understanding 38–42%; AO2 Application, analysis and evaluation 38–42%; AO3 Experimental skills, analysis and evaluation of data and methods 19–21%. Paper 1: AO1 23.2–25.7%, AO2 23.2–25.7%, AO3 11.6–12.8%; Paper 2: AO1 14.8–16.3%, AO2 14.8–16.3%, AO3 7.4–8.2%.
The specification does not state the number of multiple-choice items or any fixed mark tariff (e.g. 6-mark questions) for extended open-response questions.

command_words.Add/Label: Requires the addition or labelling of a stimulus material given in the question, for example labelling a diagram or adding units to a table.
command_words.Calculate: Obtain a numerical answer, showing relevant working.
command_words.Comment on: Requires the synthesis of a number of variables from data/information to form a judgement.
command_words.Complete: Requires the completion of a table/diagram.
command_words.Deduce: Draw/reach conclusion(s) from the information provided.
command_words.Describe: To give an account of something. Statements in the response need to be developed, as they are often linked but do not need to include a justification or reason.
command_words.Design: Plan or invent a procedure from existing principles/ideas.
command_words.Determine: The answer must have an element that is quantitative from the stimulus provided, or must show how the answer can be reached quantitatively. To gain maximum marks, there must be a quantitative element to the answer.
command_words.Discuss: Identify the issue/situation/problem/argument that is being assessed within the question. Explore all aspects of an issue/situation/problem/argument. Investigate the issue/situation etc. by reasoning or argument.
command_words.Draw: Produce a diagram using a ruler or freehand.
command_words.Estimate: Find an approximate value, number or quantity from a diagram/given data or through a calculation.
command_words.Evaluate: Review information (e.g. data, methods) then bring it together to form a conclusion, drawing on evidence including strengths, weaknesses, alternative actions, relevant data or information. Come to a supported judgement of a subject’s quality and relate it to its context.
command_words.Explain: An explanation requires a justification/exemplification of a point. The answer must contain some element of reasoning/justification – this can include mathematical explanations.
command_words.Give/State/Name: All of these command words are really synonyms. They generally all require recall of one or more pieces of information.
command_words.Give a reason/reasons: When a statement has been made and the requirement is only to give the reason(s) why.
command_words.Identify: Usually requires some key information to be selected from a given stimulus/resource.
command_words.Justify: Give evidence to support (either the statement given in the question or an earlier answer).
command_words.Plot: Produce a graph by marking points accurately on a grid from data that is provided and then draw a line of best fit through these points. A suitable scale and appropriately labelled axes must be included if these are not provided in the question.
command_words.Show that: Verify the statement given in the question.
command_words.Sketch: Produce a freehand drawing. For a graph, this would need a line and labelled axes with important features indicated. The axes are not scaled.
command_words.State what is meant by: When the meaning of a term is expected but there are different ways for how it can be described.
command_words.Suggest: Use your knowledge to propose a solution to a problem in a novel context.
command_words.Analyse the data/graph to explain: Verb preceding a command word: Examine the data/graph in detail to provide an explanation.
command_words.What, Why, Which: Direct command words used for multiple-choice questions.

given: No formula sheet, equation list, data sheet or table of constants is stated anywhere in the specification as provided in the examination (checked pp. 8-9, 11-28, 29-31 and Appendices 1-9, pp. 39-55).

Relationships worded 'use the relationship' / 'use the equation' (not 'know and use'): 1.10 v^2 = u^2 + (2 × a × s); 1.28P F = (mv − mu) / t; 2.5 E = I × V × t; 3.6 f = 1 / T; 4.17 P = W / t; 5.13P ΔQ = m × c × ΔT; 5.21 p1 / T1 = p2 / T2; 5.22 p1V1 = p2V2; 8.6 v = (2 × π × r) / T; 8.16P (λ − λ0) / λ0 = Δλ / λ0 = v / c. None of these is in the Appendix 7 'will not be provided' list (pp. 51-52), but the specification does NOT state anywhere that they are provided. Pipeline draft rule (for owner confirmation): state these in the question when needed.

No numerical value of g is stated anywhere in the specification (8.3 only says g varies and is different on other planets and the Moon); no value of the speed of light (needed for 8.16P) or of the speed of sound is stated. Any such value must be given in the question.

Calculators: 'Students will be expected to have access to a suitable electronic calculator for all examination papers'; calculators that allow retrieval of text or formulae, or with QWERTY keyboards, are not allowed (p. 30). 'A calculator may be used in the examinations' (pp. 8-9).
Appendix 8 (p. 53): 'these are the forms of circuit symbols that will be used in examination papers'; other internationally agreed symbols may be acceptable in student answers.

Appendix 7 (pp. 51-52) states: 'The relationships listed below will not be provided for students either in the form given or in rearranged form.' All 18 Appendix 7 items correspond to the 'know and use' / 'know that' statements above.

Facts stated in the content that students must know: stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance (1.19); all EM waves travel at the same speed in free space (3.10); order of the EM spectrum and colours of the visible spectrum (3.11); light waves are transverse (3.14) and sound waves longitudinal (3.23); human hearing range 20–20 000 Hz (3.24P, Paper 2 only); current is the rate of flow of charge (2.14); voltage is the energy transferred per unit charge passed and the volt is a joule per coulomb (2.20); work done is equal to energy transferred (4.12); power as the rate of transfer of energy or the rate of doing work (4.16); absolute zero is –273 °C (5.16); Kelvin temperature of a gas is proportional to the average kinetic energy of its molecules (5.19); specific heat capacity definition (5.12P, Paper 2 only); definition of half-life (7.12); fusion is the energy source for stars (7.25).
conventions: Statements in bold with a 'P' reference are International GCSE Physics only (not in Science Double Award) (p. 1); Paper 1 assesses content not in bold without a 'P' reference; Paper 2 assesses all content, including bold 'P' statements, which 'cover some sub-topics in greater depth' (pp. 8-9, 29).
Practical investigations are specification points in italics, prefixed 'practical:'; the skills are assessed through the written examinations (pp. 1, 30).

'As a minimum, all the bullet points in the content must be taught. The word 'including' in the content specifies the detail of what must be covered.' Examples ('such as', 'e.g.') are illustrative only and centres can use other examples (p. 1).

Units listed in the content: 1.1 kg, m, m/s, m/s^2, N, s, N/kg; 1.2P Nm, kg m/s (Paper 2 only); 2.1 A, C, J, Ω, s, V, W; 3.1 °, Hz, m, m/s, s; 4.1 kg, J, m, m/s, m/s^2, N, s, W; 5.1 °C, K, J, kg, kg/m^3, m, m^2, m^3, m/s, m/s^2, N, Pa; 5.2P J/kg °C (Paper 2 only); 6.1 A, V, W; 7.1 Bq, cm, h, min, s; 8.1 kg, m, m/s, m/s^2, N, s, N/kg (pp. 11-27).

Symbols as printed in the content: a, u, v, s, t, F, m, W (weight in 1.18; work done in 4.11, 4.17), g, p (momentum in 1.25P; pressure in 5.5, 5.7, 5.21, 5.22), P (power), I, V, E (energy transferred in 2.5, 2.21), Q (charge in 2.15), ΔQ (change in thermal energy in 5.13P), R, f, λ, T (time period in 3.6, 8.6; Kelvin temperature T1, T2 in 5.21), ΔT (change in temperature in 5.13P), n, i, r, c (critical angle in 3.21, 3.22; speed of light in 8.16P; specific heat capacity in 5.13P), d, h, GPE, KE, ρ, A, Vp, Ip, Vs, Is, r (orbital radius in 8.6), λ0, Δλ.
Nuclide notation: 'symbols such as ^14_6 C to describe particular nuclei' (7.2, p. 25); beta particles written β− (7.4, 7.5).

Mathematical skills (Appendix 4, pp. 45-46), ticked for Physics: 1A-1E (decimal form; standard form; ratios, fractions, percentages, powers and roots; estimates without a calculator; sin x and sin^-1 x in degrees); 2A, 2B, 2C, 2D, 2F, 2H, 2I (appropriate number of significant figures; arithmetic mean; bar charts; frequency tables, diagrams and histograms; simple probability; scatter diagrams; order of magnitude calculations) - 2E sampling and 2G mode/median are NOT ticked for Physics; 3A-3D (symbols <, >, ∝, ~; change the subject; substitute values using appropriate units; solve simple equations); 4A-4F (graphical/numerical translation; y = mx + c; plot two variables; slope and intercept; slope of a tangent as rate of change; area between curve and x-axis by counting squares); 5A-5C (angles in degrees; 2D/3D representation; areas of triangles and rectangles, surface areas and volumes of cubes).
appendices: Appendix 1: Codes (p. 39) - subject code 4PH1 (Science Double Award 4SD0); paper codes Physics Paper 1 4PH1/1P, 4SD0/1P; Physics Paper 2 4PH1/2P.
Appendix 2: World Class Qualification design principles (pp. 41-42) and Appendix 3: Transferable skills (pp. 43-44) - no assessment content.
Appendix 5: Command word taxonomy (pp. 47-48) - see command_words.
Appendix 6: Suggested practical investigations (p. 49) - 19 additional suggested investigations; these are NOT numbered specification statements and are not mapped as points.
Appendix 7: Physics formulae for relationships (pp. 51-52) - 18 relationships that 'will not be provided for students either in the form given or in rearranged form' (see not_given).

Appendix 8: Electrical circuit symbols (p. 53) - 26 symbols (shown as images): conductors crossing with no connection, junction of conductors, open switch, cell, battery of cells, power supply (DC), power supply (AC), transformer, ammeter, voltmeter, fixed resistor, variable resistor, heater, thermistor, light-dependent resistor (LDR), diode, light-emitting diode (LED), lamp, loudspeaker, microphone, electric bell, earth or ground, motor, generator, fuse/circuit breaker.
Appendix 9: Glossary (p. 55) - assessment objectives, external assessment, JCQ, linear.

points.text: explain how molecules in a gas have random motion and that they exert a force, and hence a pressure, on the walls of a container
understand why there is an absolute zero of temperature, which is –273 °C
describe the Kelvin scale of temperature and be able to convert between the Kelvin and Celsius scales
understand why an increase in temperature results in an increase in the average speed of gas molecules
know that the Kelvin temperature of a gas is proportional to the average kinetic energy of its molecules
explain, for a fixed amount of gas, the qualitative relationship between: pressure and volume at constant temperature; pressure and Kelvin temperature at constant volume
use the relationship between the pressure and Kelvin temperature of a fixed mass of gas at constant volume: p1 / T1 = p2 / T2
use the relationship between the pressure and volume of a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature: p1V1 = p2V2
use the following units: ampere (A), volt (V) and watt (W)
know that magnets repel and attract other magnets and attract magnetic substances
describe the properties of magnetically hard and soft materials
understand the term 'magnetic field line'
know that magnetism is induced in some materials when they are placed in a magnetic field
practical: investigate the magnetic field pattern for a permanent bar magnet and between two bar magnets
points.diagram_note: Practical: field patterns are usually drawn; method and pattern features can be described in words.

points.text: describe how to use two permanent magnets to produce a uniform magnetic field pattern
points.diagram_note: Uniform field between magnets is usually drawn; arrangement of poles and field describable in words.

points.text: know that an electric current in a conductor produces a magnetic field around it
describe the construction of electromagnets
points.diagram_note: Electromagnet construction is often drawn; describable in words.

points.text: draw magnetic field patterns for a straight wire, a flat circular coil and a solenoid when each is carrying a current
points.diagram_note: Drawing magnetic field patterns for a wire, coil and solenoid requires a drawn diagram.

points.text: know that there is a force on a charged particle when it moves in a magnetic field as long as its motion is not parallel to the field
understand why a force is exerted on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field and how this effect is applied in simple d.c. electric motors and loudspeakers
points.diagram_note: Motor and loudspeaker structures are often drawn; describable in words.

points.text: use the left-hand rule to predict the direction of the resulting force when a wire carries a current perpendicular to a magnetic field
points.diagram_note: Directions of current, field and force can be given in words (e.g. 'into the page').

points.text: describe how the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field changes with the magnitude and direction of the field and current

know that a voltage is induced in a conductor or a coil when it moves through a magnetic field or when a magnetic field changes through it and describe the factors that affect the size of the induced voltage

describe the generation of electricity by the rotation of a magnet within a coil of wire and of a coil of wire within a magnetic field, and describe the factors that affect the size of the induced voltage
points.diagram_note: Generator arrangements are often drawn; describable in words.

points.text: describe the structure of a transformer and understand that a transformer changes the size of an alternating voltage by having different numbers of turns on the input and output sides
points.diagram_note: Transformer structure is often drawn; describable in words.

points.text: explain the use of step-up and step-down transformers in the large-scale generation and transmission of electrical energy

know and use the relationship between input (primary) and output (secondary) voltages and the turns ratio for a transformer: input (primary) voltage / output (secondary) voltage = primary turns / secondary turns
know and use the relationship: input power = output power; VpIp = VsIs; for 100% efficiency
use the following units: becquerel (Bq), centimetre (cm), hour (h), minute (min) and second (s)
describe the structure of an atom in terms of protons, neutrons and electrons and use symbols such as ^14_6 C to describe particular nuclei
know the terms atomic (proton) number, mass (nucleon) number and isotope
know that alpha (α) particles, beta (β−) particles, and gamma (γ) rays are ionising radiations emitted from unstable nuclei in a random process
describe the nature of alpha (α) particles, beta (β−) particles and gamma (γ) rays, and recall that they may be distinguished in terms of penetrating power and ability to ionise
practical: investigate the penetration powers of different types of radiation using either radioactive sources or simulations
points.diagram_note: Practical: set-up and count-rate results can be given in words and data tables.

points.text: describe the effects on the atomic and mass numbers of a nucleus of the emission of each of the four main types of radiation (alpha, beta, gamma and neutron radiation)
understand how to balance nuclear equations in terms of mass and charge
know that photographic film or a Geiger−Müller detector can detect ionising radiations
explain the sources of background (ionising) radiation from Earth and space
know that the activity of a radioactive source decreases over a period of time and is measured in becquerels
know the definition of the term 'half-life' and understand that it is different for different radioactive isotopes
use the concept of the half-life to carry out simple calculations on activity, including graphical methods
points.diagram_note: Decay curves can be replaced by activity–time data tables.

points.text: describe uses of radioactivity in industry and medicine
describe the difference between contamination and irradiation

describe the dangers of ionising radiations, including: that radiation can cause mutations in living organisms; that radiation can damage cells and tissue; the problems arising from the disposal of radioactive waste and how the associated risks can be reduced
know that nuclear reactions, including fission, fusion and radioactive decay, can be a source of energy
understand how a nucleus of U-235 can be split (the process of fission) by collision with a neutron and that this process releases energy as kinetic energy of the fission products
know that the fission of U-235 produces two radioactive daughter nuclei and a small number of neutrons
describe how a chain reaction can be set up if the neutrons produced by one fission strike other U-235 nuclei
describe the role played by the control rods and moderator in the fission process
understand the role of shielding around a nuclear reactor
explain the difference between nuclear fusion and nuclear fission
describe nuclear fusion as the creation of larger nuclei resulting in a loss of mass from smaller nuclei, accompanied by a release of energy
know that fusion is the energy source for stars
explain why nuclear fusion does not happen at low temperatures and pressures, due to electrostatic repulsion of protons
use the following units: kilogram (kg), metre (m), metre/second (m/s), metre/second^2 (m/s^2), newton (N), second (s), newton/kilogram (N/kg)
know that: the universe is a large collection of billions of galaxies; a galaxy is a large collection of billions of stars; our solar system is in the Milky Way galaxy
understand why gravitational field strength, g, varies and know that it is different on other planets and the Moon from that on the Earth
explain that gravitational force: causes moons to orbit planets; causes the planets to orbit the Sun; causes artificial satellites to orbit the Earth; causes comets to orbit the Sun
describe the differences in the orbits of comets, moons and planets
use the relationship between orbital speed, orbital radius and time period: orbital speed = (2 × π × orbital radius) / time period; v = (2 × π × r) / T
understand how stars can be classified according to their colour
know that a star’s colour is related to its surface temperature
describe the evolution of stars of similar mass to the Sun through the following stages: nebula; star (main sequence); red giant; white dwarf
describe the evolution of stars with a mass larger than the Sun
understand how the brightness of a star at a standard distance can be represented using absolute magnitude
draw the main components of the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram (HR diagram)
points.diagram_note: Drawing the main components of the HR diagram requires a drawn diagram.

points.text: describe the past evolution of the universe and the main arguments in favour of the Big Bang theory
describe evidence that supports the Big Bang theory (red-shift and cosmic microwave background - CMB - radiation)
describe that if a wave source is moving relative to an observer, there will be a change in the observed frequency and wavelength

use the equation relating to change in wavelength, reference wavelength, velocity of a galaxy and the speed of light: change in wavelength / reference wavelength = velocity of a galaxy / speed of light; (λ − λ0) / λ0 = Δλ / λ0 = v / c
describe the red-shift in light received from galaxies at different distances away from the Earth
explain why the red-shift of galaxies provides evidence for the expansion of the universe
